title: AES-128 conditional K8[12] recovery from 13 useful faults (Giraud 2005)

target.description: Full AES-128; recover only the 8-bit byte K8[12], with the K9-tail material already available.

setting.key_relation: One fixed secret AES master key; no related-key oracle.
setting.key_population: Keys of the stated AES implementation without a weak-key restriction; fault protections are outside the model.
setting.plaintext_model: Repeat encryptions of the same plaintext under the same key; retain its correct ciphertext as a reference. Counts of faulty ciphertexts exclude that reusable reference unless explicitly stated otherwise.

fault_model.target: Byte K8[12], the case whose fault difference cannot be directly recovered from one output difference.
fault_model.granularity: One initially affected byte, followed by propagation through the key schedule or AES rounds.
fault_model.timing: After the correct K8 addition and before online K9 derivation.
fault_model.location: Count only useful outputs from faults on K8[12]; position acquisition or rejection cost is excluded.
fault_model.value_control: The byte difference is unknown; its value may be inferred or guessed from correct/faulty outputs. Eq19 enumerates unknown fault masks, not key candidates:107–146 possibilities, mean126.50390625 over uniform output deltas; the source≈127 remains an approximation.
fault_model.sample_pairing: Every faulty output is matched to the same fixed-input correct reference; useful faults, random-location ciphertexts and physical executions have distinct accounting.

assumptions: A round key is used correctly for encryption and then faulted before generating the next round key. The implementation expands keys on the fly.
The reported outcome and data budget use the paper's candidate-filtering model; no numerical whole-key success rate is inferred from a byte-level statistic.
This is a conditional stage, not an attack starting with no known subkey material.
Eq.(19) leaves 107–146 possible fault differences, about 127 on average. These are fault-value candidates, not key candidates.

prior_key_knowledge.material: K9[12..15] from the preceding stage; the local equation uses the corresponding K9[k].
prior_key_knowledge.cost_accounting: The listed stage budget excludes acquisition of this prior subkey material; the upstream recovery must be costed separately.

time.note: No numerical whole-endpoint runtime is reported for this version and endpoint.

data.note: Same plaintext and target byte; excludes the upstream K9-tail recovery and acquisition of faults at the desired position.

memory.note: The article describes counters or candidate lists without a numerical peak-memory budget.

preprocessing.note: No separate reusable preprocessing-time budget is reported. The Appendix A 8×2^8 equation tests per useful output are a component count, not a complete attack cost.

success.description: Approximately 99% reported from simulations with 13 useful faulty outputs. Trial count and confidence interval are unspecified; this is not full-key success.

evidence.interpretation: Version-specific endpoint retaining its target, prior information, fault controls and native sample accounting.

evidence.locator: Complete proceedingsPDF1–15/printed27–41 and earlyPS15-page reading rendition; Sections3–6, AppendixA and references.
evidence.interpretation: Full exact-edition text and AES contribution inventory reviewed; component checks and whole-attack reproduction are separate.

limitations: Useful faulty ciphertext counts do not automatically include ineffective physical injections or calibration attempts.
The article does not supply a measured success frequency, runtime or peak memory for every target and parameter choice.

The exactly-one-zero output test can reject valid tail faults with extra zero differences. Independent finite valid-key cases find94 such rejections among16320 tail faults;48960 sampled non-tail faults give no false accepts, not a universal soundness proof. Keep reported useful-sample versus acquisition counts distinct.
